interactions.label: Why do gut movements continue even when a patient is under general anaesthesia?

params.question: Why do gut movements continue even when a patient is under general anaesthesia?

answers.text: Gut smooth muscle contracts autonomously without any neural input

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Smooth muscle has intrinsic rhythmicity, but coordinated peristalsis requires neural control. The enteric nervous system provides this coordination independently of the CNS.

answers.text: The enteric nervous system can function independently of the brain and spinal cord

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The enteric nervous system — Meissner's and Auerbach's plexuses containing about 500 million neurons — operates as an independent network, earning it the name 'the second brain.'

answers.text: Sympathetic nerve fibres are resistant to anaesthetic agents

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sympathetic fibres actually inhibit gut motility. Even if they were resistant to anaesthesia, their activity would suppress peristalsis, not sustain it.

answers.text: Circulating gastrointestinal hormones maintain peristalsis during anaesthesia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While GI hormones like motilin modulate motility, the primary reason gut movements persist under anaesthesia is the independent functioning of the intrinsic enteric nervous system.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key concept is that the enteric nervous system (Meissner's and Auerbach's plexuses) contains ~500 million neurons and can function independently of the CNS — which is why peristalsis continues under general anaesthesia.
The enteric nervous system is the 'second brain' — an independent network of ~500 million neurons that coordinates gut movements without requiring input from the brain or spinal cord.

interactions.label: What makes saliva unique among all gastrointestinal secretions?

params.question: What makes saliva unique among all gastrointestinal secretions?

answers.text: It contains digestive enzymes that act at an acidic pH

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Salivary amylase acts at a near-neutral pH of about 6.8, not acidic. Pepsin in gastric juice is the enzyme that functions at acidic pH.

answers.text: It is the only GI secretion regulated entirely by hormones

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The opposite is true — salivation is controlled entirely by the nervous system, with no hormonal input. This is itself a unique feature of salivary regulation.

answers.text: It is hypotonic, unlike all other GI secretions which are isotonic or hypertonic

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Acinar cells produce isotonic fluid, but striated ducts reabsorb sodium and secrete potassium. The final saliva is hypotonic — a feature unique to saliva among all GI secretions.

answers.text: It is produced at the highest daily volume of any digestive secretion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Saliva output is 1–1.5 litres per day. Both gastric juice (2–3 L/day) and pancreatic juice (up to 2.5 L/day) exceed this volume.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key fact is that saliva is the only hypotonic GI secretion. Acinar cells produce isotonic fluid, but striated ducts modify it by reabsorbing sodium and secreting potassium, making the final product hypotonic.
Saliva's hypotonic nature results from ductal modification — Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion by striated ducts transform the isotonic acinar fluid into a uniquely hypotonic secretion.

interactions.label: If enterokinase were produced within the pancreas itself rather than the duodena

params.question: If enterokinase were produced within the pancreas itself rather than the duodenal mucosa, the risk of pancreatic autodigestion would increase.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. Enterokinase is deliberately produced only in the duodenal mucosa, not the pancreas. If it were produced inside the pancreas, trypsinogen would be converted to trypsin prematurely, initiating a protease cascade that could digest pancreatic tissue — essentially what happens in acute pancreatitis.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Enterokinase is produced only in the duodenal mucosa. This spatial separation is the key safety mechanism — if enterokinase were inside the pancreas, it would convert trypsinogen to trypsin prematurely, triggering a protease cascade that could digest pancreatic tissue. This is essentially the mechanism behind acute pancreatitis.

interactions.label: After digestion and absorption into enterocytes, dietary fat is repackaged into

params.question: After digestion and absorption into enterocytes, dietary fat is repackaged into chylomicrons and released into which vessels?

answers.text: Branches of the hepatic portal vein

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The hepatic portal vein carries water-soluble nutrients such as amino acids and monosaccharides. Dietary fat in chylomicrons bypasses portal circulation entirely.

answers.text: Mesenteric arterioles

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Arterioles supply oxygenated blood to the intestinal wall. They do not receive absorbed nutrients — absorption occurs into capillaries and lacteals, not arterioles.

answers.text: Submucosal venules draining into the inferior vena cava

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Submucosal venules drain into the portal system and carry water-soluble nutrients to the liver. Chylomicrons take the lymphatic route, not the venous route.

answers.text: Lymphatic lacteals in the villi

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Inside enterocytes, fats are rebuilt into triglycerides, packaged into chylomicrons, and released into lacteals — the lymphatic vessels of the villi. They then travel via the thoracic duct to the systemic circulation, bypassing the liver on first pass.

overallFeedback.feedback: Unlike amino acids and monosaccharides that enter portal blood, dietary fat is packaged into chylomicrons and released into lacteals (lymphatic vessels in the villi), travelling via the thoracic duct to the systemic circulation.

Dietary fat takes a unique route: after re-esterification and packaging into chylomicrons within enterocytes, it enters lacteals and travels via the lymphatic system to the systemic circulation — bypassing the liver's first-pass metabolism.

interactions.label: Why is ALT considered more specific than AST as a marker for hepatocellular dama

params.question: Why is ALT considered more specific than AST as a marker for hepatocellular damage?

answers.text: ALT is found predominantly in hepatocytes, while AST is also present in skeletal and cardiac muscle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. ALT is predominantly a hepatocyte enzyme, so its elevation points specifically to liver injury. AST is present in multiple tissues including skeletal and cardiac muscle, so it can be raised by non-hepatic causes such as myocardial infarction or rhabdomyolysis.

answers.text: ALT is directly involved in bilirubin conjugation within the hepatocyte

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ALT is a transaminase involved in amino acid metabolism, not bilirubin conjugation. Bilirubin conjugation is carried out by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase in the hepatocyte.

answers.text: AST is rapidly cleared from the blood, making it unreliable for measuring liver damage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both ALT and AST have clinically useful half-lives in blood. The difference in specificity is due to tissue distribution, not clearance rates.

answers.text: ALT rises earlier than AST after hepatocellular injury, providing a faster diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both enzymes rise rapidly after hepatocellular damage. The advantage of ALT is its tissue specificity — it more reliably points to the liver as the source — not its speed of rise.

overallFeedback.feedback: ALT is more specific than AST for liver damage because it is found predominantly in hepatocytes. AST is present in multiple tissues including muscle, so its elevation can have non-hepatic causes — making it less specific for the liver.

ALT's specificity for hepatocellular damage comes from its tissue distribution — it is predominantly a hepatocyte enzyme. AST, while also elevated in hepatitis, can be raised by skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and other tissue injuries.

interactions.label: A patient has profuse watery diarrhoea that does not stop even when oral intake

params.question: A patient has profuse watery diarrhoea that does not stop even when oral intake is completely withheld. Which type of diarrhoea does this pattern indicate?

answers.text: Osmotic diarrhoea

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Osmotic diarrhoea is caused by unabsorbed solutes drawing water into the lumen. It characteristically stops when the patient fasts, because the osmotic load is removed. Persistence during fasting rules it out.

answers.text: Secretory diarrhoea

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In secretory diarrhoea, as in cholera, the intestinal epithelium actively secretes chloride and water regardless of luminal contents. This is why it persists even during fasting — the secretion is independent of dietary intake.

answers.text: Inflammatory diarrhoea

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Inflammatory diarrhoea typically presents with blood or mucus in the stool due to mucosal damage. Profuse watery diarrhoea persisting during fasting points to a secretory mechanism.

answers.text: Malabsorptive diarrhoea

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Malabsorptive diarrhoea is characterised by steatorrhoea — fatty, foul-smelling stools from poor fat absorption. It improves with fasting as there is less fat to malabsorb.

overallFeedback.feedback: Diarrhoea that persists during fasting indicates a secretory mechanism — the intestinal epithelium is actively secreting fluid regardless of luminal contents. In cholera, the toxin locks on chloride secretion via cAMP, producing massive watery output even without oral intake.

The fasting test is a key clinical distinction: secretory diarrhoea persists during fasting because active intestinal secretion is independent of dietary input, whereas osmotic diarrhoea stops when the osmotic load is removed.
